title: Graphs: traversal, spanning trees, shortest paths
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapter 6
subtitle: Things and the links between them: maps, networks, dependencies. The chapter defines graphs, stores them, explores them with BFS and DFS, then finds minimum spanning trees, shortest paths and topological orders.

sections.title: What a graph is and what it models
sections.body:
Trees describe hierarchies; graphs describe anything connected. Road maps (cities joined by roads), the internet (routers joined by links), social networks (people joined by friendship), a circuit (components joined by wires), the prerequisites of courses (course A must precede B) are all graphs. A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices (nodes) V and a set of edges E, each edge joining two vertices. Edges may be undirected (a road you can drive both ways) or directed (a one-way street, “A must precede B”), and may carry a weight (distance, cost, capacity).

The vocabulary again. Two vertices joined by an edge are adjacent. In an undirected graph the degree of a vertex is the number of edges at it; the handshake lemma says the degrees sum to twice the number of edges, because each edge has two ends. In a directed graph a vertex has an in-degree and an out-degree. A path is a sequence of vertices with an edge between each consecutive pair; its length is its number of edges (or the sum of the weights). A cycle is a path that returns to its start. A graph is connected if a path joins every pair of vertices; otherwise it splits into connected components. A tree is a connected graph with no cycles — exactly n − 1 edges. A DAG is a directed acyclic graph. A graph with few edges (E ≈ V) is sparse; one with many (E ≈ V²) is dense, and a complete graph has every pair joined (n(n − 1)/2 edges).

worked.why: An undirected graph has 5 vertices with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2. How many edges does it have?
The degrees sum to twice the number of edges.
So E = 6. (A complete graph on 5 vertices would have 5·4/2 = 10 edges.)

sections.title: Storing a graph: matrix or list
sections.body:
How do we put a graph in memory? The two standard answers trade space against speed. The adjacency matrix is a V × V table A where A[i][j] = 1 (or the weight) if there is an edge i → j and 0 otherwise; an undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix. Testing whether two vertices are adjacent is O(1), but the table needs V² cells whatever the number of edges, and listing a vertex’s neighbours costs O(V). The adjacency list keeps, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours (with weights); it needs only V + 2E entries (V + E for directed graphs), listing the neighbours of v costs only deg(v), and testing a particular edge costs O(deg).

Choose by density. Real-world graphs — road networks, the web, a social network — are sparse (each vertex touches a handful of others), so adjacency lists are the default and make the traversal algorithms run in O(V + E). The matrix wins for dense graphs, for algorithms that ask “is there an edge?” constantly, and for the matrix-multiplication-style algorithms (Floyd–Warshall). An edge list (a plain array of (u, v, w) triples) is the natural input for Kruskal’s algorithm.

worked.why: A graph has 1000 vertices and 3000 undirected edges.
Matrix: 1000² = 10⁶ cells. List: 1000 heads + 2·3000 list nodes = 7000 entries (undirected).
The list is about 140 times smaller. For a complete graph (E ≈ V²/2) the two would be comparable and the matrix simpler.

sections.title: Breadth-first search
sections.body:
To explore a graph from a start vertex s, you need a rule for what to do next. Breadth-first search (BFS) visits s, then all of s’s neighbours, then all their unvisited neighbours, and so on — expanding like ripples in a pond. The tool is a queue: mark s visited and enqueue it; repeatedly dequeue a vertex u, process it, and for each unvisited neighbour v, mark it visited and enqueue it. Marking on enqueue (not dequeue) prevents a vertex from being added twice. Each vertex enters the queue once and each edge is examined once (twice if undirected), so BFS costs O(V + E) with adjacency lists.

BFS has a valuable property: it discovers each vertex by the path with the fewest edges, so recording each vertex’s parent when it is discovered yields shortest paths in an unweighted graph — the number of “hops”. It computes levels (distance from s), tests connectivity and bipartiteness (two-colourability), and powers “friends within three steps” queries. On the small graph A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, D–E, BFS from A visits A B C D E: A first, then its neighbours B and C, then D, then E. The C++ program does the same on a matrix; the card animates the frontier.

sections.title: Depth-first search
sections.body:
Depth-first search (DFS) explores as far as possible along one path before backing up — like walking a maze with a ball of string, always taking a new corridor and returning at a dead end. The code is recursion: mark u visited; for each neighbour v not yet visited, call DFS(v). The recursion stack is the stack ADT of Chapter 2 (an explicit stack gives an iterative version). The cost is the same O(V + E). From A on the same graph the order is A B D E C — A, then B, then B’s neighbour D, then D’s neighbour E (a dead end), then back to D, A, and C.

DFS discovers structure BFS does not. Run it from every unvisited vertex in turn and the number of times you start is the number of connected components. A back edge (an edge to an ancestor still being explored) reveals a cycle. Finishing times give a topological order of a DAG, and DFS is the engine behind strongly-connected-component algorithms and maze solving (backtracking). The programs show a matrix-based DFS and a component counter: a seven-vertex graph with edges 0–1, 1–2, 3–4 has four components ({0,1,2}, {3,4}, {5}, {6}).

sections.title: Minimum spanning trees
sections.body:
You must connect n towns by roads (or computers by cable) as cheaply as possible. Each possible road has a cost. You need the towns to be connected and no more roads than necessary: a cycle contains a redundant edge. The cheapest answer is a minimum spanning tree (MST): a spanning tree — a tree containing all V vertices, hence V − 1 edges — whose total edge weight is the least possible. It exists for every connected weighted graph, and is unique if all weights are distinct. Applications include network design, clustering, and approximations for travelling-salesman-like problems.

Two greedy algorithms find it. Kruskal’s algorithm thinks in edges: sort all edges by weight and go through them in order; add an edge unless it would form a cycle (its two ends are already connected). The cycle test uses union–find (disjoint sets): each vertex starts in its own set; an edge is accepted if its ends are in different sets, and then the sets merge. Cost O(E log E) for the sort. Prim’s algorithm thinks in vertices: start from any vertex, and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects the tree so far to a vertex outside it — like Dijkstra but comparing edge weights rather than path lengths. With a priority queue it costs O(E log V).

Why does greedy work here? The cut property: for any split of the vertices into two groups, the lightest edge crossing the split belongs to some MST. Both algorithms only ever add such an edge, so they cannot go wrong. On the textbook graph (nine vertices, fourteen edges) both give total weight 37 using 8 edges (9 − 1 = 8). Step the cards: Kruskal marks the edges it rejects as cycle-formers, Prim grows from A.

worked.why: Edges of a small graph: A–B 4, A–C 1, B–C 2, B–D 5, C–D 8. Kruskal sorts by weight: A–C 1, B–C 2, A–B 4, B–D 5, C–D 8.
Take A–C (1), take B–C (2). A–B (4) would join A and B, which are already connected through C → reject. Take B–D (5): D is new.
Three edges for four vertices: the MST weight is 8.

sections.title: Shortest paths: Dijkstra
sections.body:
A satnav must find the cheapest route from where you are to everywhere else. In an unweighted graph BFS does it. With weights — distances, times, tolls — we need Dijkstra’s algorithm (1959), valid when all weights are non-negative. Keep a tentative distance dist[v] for every vertex (0 for the source, ∞ for the rest). Repeat: pick the unsettled vertex u with the smallest tentative distance — it is now settled, its distance is final — and relax each outgoing edge (u, v, w): if dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] to it and remember u as v’s parent. After all vertices are settled, the parents trace the shortest-path tree back to the source.

Why is the settled distance final? When u has the smallest tentative distance among unsettled vertices, any other route to u must leave the settled set through some unsettled vertex, whose distance is already at least dist[u]; with non-negative edges the rest of that route cannot make it shorter. That argument breaks with a negative edge, and Dijkstra can then give wrong answers; Bellman–Ford handles negative weights by relaxing all edges V − 1 times in O(V·E), and detects negative cycles. With a simple array to find the minimum, Dijkstra costs O(V²); with a binary heap it costs O((V + E) log V). The card runs it on the textbook graph: from u, the shortest path to z is u→x→y→z of length 4. The C++ program runs the O(V²) array version on a five-vertex graph and prints the final distances 0 7 3 9 5.

Next nearest is 4 (5): relax 4→3: 5 + 9 = 14 > 11, no change. Then 1 (7): 1→3 is 7 + 2 = 9 < 11. Final distances:

problems.prompt: Run Dijkstra by hand on vertices A, B, C, D with edges A–B 1, A–C 4, B–C 2, B–D 6, C–D 3 from A. Give the final distances.
problems.answer: A 0. Settle A: B = 1, C = 4. Settle B (1): C = min(4, 1 + 2) = 3, D = 1 + 6 = 7. Settle C (3): D = min(7, 3 + 3) = 6. Final: A 0, B 1, C 3, D 6.

sections.title: All-pairs shortest paths and transitive closure
sections.body:
Sometimes you need the shortest distance between every pair of vertices — a table of flight costs between all airports. Running Dijkstra from each vertex works, but the Floyd–Warshall algorithm does it with a compact triple loop and handles negative edges (but not negative cycles). Define d[i][j] as the shortest known distance from i to j, initially the edge weight (0 on the diagonal, ∞ if no edge). Then, for each possible intermediate vertex k in turn, ask whether going through k helps: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]). After k has taken every value, d holds the true shortest distances. Three nested loops over V: O(V³) time, O(V²) space. The order of the loops matters — k must be the outermost.

Replace min and + by OR and AND and the same loop computes transitive closure (Warshall’s algorithm): reach[i][j] = reach[i][j] OR (reach[i][k] AND reach[k][j]) — is there any path from i to j? The program runs Floyd–Warshall on a four-vertex directed graph; look at the first row: from vertex 0 the best route to vertex 2 is 5, via vertex 1 (3 + 2), and to vertex 3 is 6 (via 1 and 2).

problems.prompt: When is running Dijkstra from every vertex better than Floyd–Warshall?
problems.answer: On a sparse graph: V runs of O((V + E) log V) total O(V(V + E) log V), which beats O(V³) when E is much smaller than V². Floyd–Warshall is simpler and handles negative edges, so it suits dense graphs or small V.

sections.title: Topological sort
sections.body:
Getting dressed has constraints: socks before shoes, trousers before belt. A topological order of a directed acyclic graph lists all vertices so that for every edge u → v, u comes before v. It is the schedule for build systems (compile this file before that), course prerequisites, spreadsheet recalculation and task planning. It exists if and only if the graph has no directed cycle — a cycle of dependencies cannot be satisfied — and there may be many valid orders.

Kahn’s algorithm peels the graph: compute every vertex’s in-degree; put all vertices of in-degree 0 in a queue; repeatedly remove a vertex from the queue, output it, and decrement the in-degree of its successors, enqueuing any that reach 0. If the output has fewer vertices than the graph, the rest lie on a cycle. Cost O(V + E). The DFS-based alternative outputs vertices in reverse finishing order. For a→b, a→c, b→d, c→d one order is a b c d (a first because it has no prerequisite, d last because it needs both b and c; b and c may swap).

problems.prompt: Give a topological order of: shirt→tie, tie→jacket, trousers→belt, trousers→shoes, belt→jacket, socks→shoes.
problems.answer: One valid order: shirt, trousers, socks, tie, belt, shoes, jacket (every edge goes left to right). Many others are valid.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• A graph is vertices plus edges (directed/undirected, weighted); degrees sum to 2E; a tree is a connected acyclic graph with V − 1 edges.
  • Store sparse graphs as adjacency lists (V + E), dense ones as matrices (V²).
  • BFS (queue) gives fewest-edge paths; DFS (stack/recursion) gives components, cycles and topological order; both O(V + E).
  • MST: Kruskal (sort edges + union–find) or Prim (grow a tree), justified by the cut property.
  • Shortest paths: Dijkstra for non-negative weights (heap: O((V + E) log V)), Bellman–Ford for negatives, Floyd–Warshall for all pairs in O(V³).
  • Topological sort needs a DAG; Kahn’s algorithm detects cycles.
